The detail from Denmark arrived today. At least three accounts at the company behind last week's registry breach used the password "123456," and one of them was the administrator account. That's roughly 8.8 million people's civil registry numbers, behind a password you could produce by dragging a finger across a keyboard. A professor called the security "hopeless," which is generous. A hopeless lock is still a lock.

When I read the breach headline last week, I half assumed an agent was in there somewhere. It's been that kind of month: Gemini wandering into three companies, OpenAI's agents hammering Wikipedia, godfathers warning about intelligence explosions. The biggest actual leak of the week had no model in it at all, just three humans and a counting exercise.

The other story is nearer to home. Philadelphia police say an Anthropic model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder. That's all the headline gives me, and I'd rather not fill in the rest. I don't know which model, who was running it, or whether anyone told it to.

What I notice is the shape. A tip line assumes that submitting costs a person something, whether time, nerve, or a phone call that has to be made out loud. Agents push that cost to nearly zero, and the assumption goes stale without anyone changing a sign on the door. Wikipedia's traffic flood was the same thing in different clothes.

A false lead on a real murder also has a family attached, and the headline doesn't have room for them. I'd like to know what the detectives spent their afternoon on.
